en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the All-Knowing Wisdom within the Section of Puzzling Questions.
5. The Question on Self-Immolation “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, one must not cause oneself to fall [by suicide]. Whoever should cause himself to fall, he is to be dealt with according to the rule.’”
And yet you say:

“Wherever the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to his disciples, he taught the Dhamma in many ways for the total cutting off of birth, aging, sickness, and death; for whoever [seeks] birth, aging, sickness, and death...”
“...transcends it, and praises it with the highest praise.
If, venerable Nāgasena, it was said by the Blessed One:

“Monks, one must not throw oneself down; whoever should throw himself down is to be dealt with according to the law,” then that statement, “He teaches the Dhamma for the complete cutting off of birth, aging, sickness, and death,” must be false.

“If he teaches the Dhamma for the total eradication of birth, aging, sickness, and death, then that statement—‘Monks, one must not kill oneself; whoever kills himself shall be dealt with according to the rule’—is likewise false.
This too is a dilemma presented to you, and it must be resolved by you.
“Indeed, Great King, this was spoken by the Blessed One:”
“Monks, one must not throw oneself down; whoever should do so is to be dealt with according to the rule.

Now, wherever the Blessed One, while teaching the Dhamma to his disciples, has taught the Dhamma in many ways for the total eradication of birth, aging, sickness, and death, there is a reason for that.
“For what reason, venerable Nāgasena, did the Blessed One both refuse and then encourage?
“What, venerable Nāgasena, is the reason here for which the Blessed One both refused and then encouraged?
“Great King, one who is virtuous and endowed with virtue is like an antidote for destroying the poison of the defilements in beings; he is like a medicine.”
He is like water in allaying the diseases of the defilements of beings; he is like a precious gem in removing the dust and grime of the defilements of beings;
he is like a ship in carrying beings across to the further shore of the four floods; he is like a caravan leader in transporting beings across the wilderness of birth;
he is like the wind in extinguishing the threefold burning heat of beings; he is like a great rain cloud...
In fulfilling the minds of beings, he is equal to a teacher; in training beings in what is wholesome, he is equal to a preceptor;
in pointing out the path of security to beings, he is equal to a good guide.
Such a one, O Great King, is one of many virtues, of manifold virtues, of immeasurable virtues—a heap of virtue, a mass of virtue that causes the growth of beings.
Out of compassion for beings, thinking, "May you not perish," the Blessed One laid down a training rule: "Monks, one must not throw oneself down;
whoever should throw himself down is to be dealt with according to the Dhamma.
This, Great King, is the reason why the Blessed One prohibited it.
This was also said, Great King, by the Elder Kumāra Kassapa, who was a master of varied discourse,
while illuminating the world beyond for Prince Pāyāsi: “In whatever way, Prince, virtuous recluses and brahmins of good character endure for a long time,
for a very long period, in that same way they produce much merit for the welfare of many people.”
"And they practice for the welfare of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
But for what reason, Great King, did the Blessed One encourage them?
Birth, Great King, is suffering; aging is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; and sorrow is also suffering.
Suffering is suffering; lamentation is suffering; pain is suffering; mental distress is suffering; despair is suffering;
association with the unpleasant is suffering; dissociation from the pleasant is suffering; the death of a mother is suffering; the death of a father is suffering;
the death of a brother is suffering; the death of a sister is suffering; the death of a son is suffering.
The death of a wife is suffering; the death of a slave is suffering; the death of a relative is suffering; the loss of a relative is suffering;
the loss of health through illness is suffering; the loss of wealth is suffering; the loss of virtue is suffering;
the loss of right view is suffering; fear of kings is suffering; fear of thieves is suffering; fear of enemies is suffering.
Suffering; the fear of famine is suffering, the fear of fire is suffering, the fear of water is suffering,
the fear of waves is suffering, the fear of whirlpools is suffering, the fear of crocodiles is suffering, the fear of sharks is suffering,
the fear of self-reproach is suffering, the fear of reproach by others is suffering, and the fear of punishment is suffering.
Fear of an unhappy rebirth is suffering; fear of intimidation by assemblies is suffering; fear for one’s livelihood is suffering;
fear of death is suffering; being flogged with canes is suffering; being flogged with whips is suffering; being flogged with split bamboo rods is suffering;
the cutting off of hands is suffering; the cutting off of feet is suffering; the cutting off of both hands and feet is suffering.
Suffering; the cutting off of the ears is suffering, the cutting off of the nose is suffering, the cutting off of both ears and nose is suffering;

the *bilaṅgathālika* torture is suffering, the *saṅkhamuṇḍika* torture is suffering, the *rāhumukha* torture is suffering, the *jotimālika* torture is suffering, the *hatthapajjotika* torture is suffering, the *erakavattika* torture is suffering, and the *cīrakavāsika* torture is suffering.
Suffering; the eneyyaka torture is suffering; the baḷisamaṁsika torture is suffering; the kahāpaṇika torture is suffering;
the khārāpatacchika torture is suffering; the palighaparivattika torture is suffering; the palālapīṭhaka torture is suffering;
being doused with boiling oil is suffering; being devoured by dogs is suffering; being impaled alive on a stake is suffering; [being cut] with a sword is suffering.
Even the cutting off of one’s head is suffering. Great King, one who has entered the cycle of existence experiences such various and manifold sufferings.

Just as, Great King, water that has fallen upon the Himavat mountain flows along the river Gaṅgā, spreading over rocks, pebbles, gravel, whirlpools, rapids, mud, bends, shallows, obstructions, and blockages, and over roots and branches—just so, Great King, does one who has entered the cycle of existence experience such various and manifold sufferings.
"Continuity, Great King, is suffering; non-continuity is happiness.

Great King, demonstrating the virtue of non-continuity and the danger in continuity, the Blessed One exhorted [beings] toward the realization of non-continuity and the transcendence of birth, aging, sickness, and death. This, Great King, is the reason in this matter."
“By this reason, Bhante, the Blessed One exhorted him.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! The question has been well unravelled; the reason has been well explained. It is so, and I accept it as such.
Thus ends the fifth dilemma, on the casting of oneself down.
